title: China Isn't Scared of Trump's Squeeze on Iran
gist: Two Washington Institute analysts argue Treasury Secretary Bessent's new 'economic D-Day' sanctions campaign against Iran has a fatal design flaw — it deliberately avoids naming China, which buys roughly 90% of Iran's oil and holds a rare-earths export weapon that already forced a U.S. tariff climbdown once — meaning the pressure campaign will stay half-hearted as long as Washington wants to protect the planned Trump-Xi summit.

themes.theme: China as Iran's real economic lifeline

insights.claim: China is the largest buyer of Iranian oil, with some estimates putting roughly 90 percent of Iran's oil exports shipped there through a network of 'shadow fleets,' and China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which enables bank transfers outside the U.S. dollar system, has seen daily transaction volumes rise from 680 billion RMB to 790 billion RMB since the Iran war began.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: A ~16% rise in CIPS daily volume since the Iran war's start is a concrete, trackable proxy for the scale of dollar-system sanctions evasion flowing through Chinese payment rails — a leading indicator of de-dollarization momentum tied directly to sanctions pressure.
insights.locator: China has long been the largest buyer of Iranian oil

insights.claim: The authors argue there is a 'fatal flaw' in the Trump administration's 'economic D-Day' sanctions campaign against Iran: Treasury Secretary Bessent declared the goal was to 'sever every economic lifeline' sustaining the regime, but did not name China, Iran's single greatest economic lifeline.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: Sets the article's core investment-relevant thesis: any Iran sanctions escalation that omits China is structurally unable to materially cut Iranian oil revenue, implying continued baseline Iranian oil-export flows to price into crude supply forecasts.
insights.quote: sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime
insights.locator: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared

insights.claim: When pressed at a press conference on whether the sanctions campaign would target Beijing, Bessent demurred without naming China, saying only 'No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,' and when asked why Treasury was issuing a threat rather than immediately imposing sanctions, replied, 'Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?'
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: Bessent's own words reveal the administration is consciously avoiding a China-targeted sanctions shock that could destabilize the global financial system — a direct admission that the campaign's scope is capped for macro-stability reasons.
insights.quote: Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?
insights.locator: when pressed on why the Treasury Department is issuing a threat

insights.claim: The new U.S. sanctions package targets 60 smaller intermediary firms and follows earlier sanctions on one major Chinese independent refinery and 40 shipping firms, but has not yet gone after the larger Chinese banks that support these refineries or the broader financial system funneling funds to Iran.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: The specific gap — sanctioning intermediaries and shippers but not core Chinese banking infrastructure — is the concrete tell that the campaign is scoped to avoid real escalation; watch for any future move against major Chinese banks as the actual escalation signal.
insights.locator: the U.S. hasn't yet gone after the more significant Chinese banks

insights.claim: In May 2026, China invoked for the first time its new 'blocking rules,' a legal framework prohibiting any company inside or outside China from complying with U.S. sanctions on Iran, in response to U.S. sanctions on several of its largest independent oil refineries; China has not yet enforced the rule but continues signaling readiness to do so.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: China's 'blocking rules' are a legal counter-sanctions mechanism that could be activated at any point to shield Chinese and even foreign firms from complying with U.S. Iran sanctions — a specific tool to monitor for escalation.
insights.locator: Beijing has recently armed itself with a legal framework for retaliation.

insights.claim: China's 'ace in the hole' is its ability to ban rare-earths exports again; freezing rare-earths exports to the U.S. last year brought parts of U.S. manufacturing, particularly the defense sector, to a standstill and forced a rapid climbdown by Trump on Chinese tariffs.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: A documented precedent of a rare-earths export freeze already forcing a U.S. tariff reversal establishes China's rare-earths leverage as a proven, not theoretical, deterrent against further U.S. sanctions escalation — a key risk factor for U.S. defense-sector supply chains.
insights.locator: Freezing exports of rare earths to the U.S. last year

insights.claim: The U.S. has struggled to build alternative rare-earths supply chains because it is competing against decades of Chinese refining investment, and because the U.S. had willingly offshored much of this refining capacity due to its highly polluting nature.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: A structural, multi-decade reason (not just policy neglect) why U.S. rare-earths self-sufficiency remains distant — relevant for sizing the realistic timeline of any Western rare-earths supply-chain diversification investment thesis.
insights.locator: The U.S. has made grand statements about developing alternative supply chains

themes.theme: Xi's priority is economic stability, not Iran

insights.claim: Xi Jinping needs economic stability to continue reforming China's economy away from export reliance toward domestic demand, following the impact of COVID and the collapse of the property bubble — which requires a stable relationship with the U.S., and explains why Beijing is working to keep the planned September Trump-Xi summit on track.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: China's domestic economic-rebalancing priority is the structural reason it will avoid escalating over Iran — implying the September Trump-Xi summit is a more reliable near-term catalyst to watch than the Iran sanctions fight itself.

insights.claim: The authors predict that neither China nor the U.S. is willing to reignite the trade war or escalate tensions over Iran, meaning Beijing views the sanctions campaign as, at most, a distraction from the more important bilateral trade relationship, not a serious threat.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: A clear directional prediction: expect continued de-escalatory signaling between Washington and Beijing on trade even amid Iran sanctions rhetoric — relevant for positioning around U.S.-China trade-war tail risk.
insights.locator: neither China nor the U.S. appears willing to reignite the trade war

insights.claim: The authors argue this dynamic may ultimately benefit Iran: if the U.S. cannot or will not bring serious economic pressure to bear on China (Iran's chief economic lifeline), it will have to rely on port blockades and military pressure alone, which have a decades-long track record of Iranian resilience.
insights.speaker: Henry Tugendhat, Grant Rumley
insights.so_what: Implies Iranian oil export volumes and regime economic resilience are likely to remain higher than headline U.S. sanctions rhetoric would suggest — a relevant calibration for oil-supply and Iran-risk-premium forecasting.
insights.locator: This dynamic may ultimately benefit Iran.
